title: People Scientist
goal: Your kid runs the scientific method on everyday people, with small, kind experiments. They notice a pattern in how people behave, predict what will happen, test it with something friendly like saying hi first, count the results honestly, and figure out why people reacted the way they did.
need: A walking path, a street, a market or a park
A notebook and a pencil for tally marks
Ten to twenty minutes, a few different days

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is turning people into test subjects. Your job is to keep every experiment kind, stay right beside them, and help them treat a 'no answer' as data, not as a rejection.

plan.what: Notice a pattern and make a prediction (Steps 1 and 2).
Run the test and count (Steps 3 and 4).
Explain the results, then plan the next test (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: Nobody answers, and they feel embarrassed
troubleshoot.a: Zero is a result too. Write it down, and ask what might explain it. Real scientists get surprising results all the time.

troubleshoot.q: They're too shy to go first
troubleshoot.a: Do the test together the first time, side by side, then let them take over the counting, or the saying hi.
Keep experiments to a friendly hi, a smile or a held door, in public places, with you right there. No personal questions, no following anyone.

lesson.text: A good people scientist turns 'people here are weird' into a question they can test. They predict, test with something kind, count what really happens, and only then decide what it means. The surprises are usually the best part.

model.line: At home, people say hi on the path. Here, they look down.
We say hi first to everyone we cross.
Some answer. Some look puzzled first, then answer.
Maybe they're friendly, just not used to saying hi.

lesson.modelNote: The puzzled faces were the real discovery. People weren't unfriendly. Saying hi to strangers just wasn't the habit there, and many answered once someone went first.

steps.title: Notice a pattern
steps.why: Every experiment starts with something you noticed. People do the same things over and over, if you watch.
steps.kid: Your kid watches people in one place, like a path, a market or a park, and writes one thing they seem to do a lot, using the Questions to test card in the People Scientist Toolkit at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Wonder out loud together: 'Have you noticed that nobody here says hi?' or 'Why does everyone wave on this path?'
ask: What do people here do a lot?
Is it the same at home, or different?
steps.tip: New places are the best labs. Something that feels strange when you travel is usually a pattern worth testing.

levels.explore: Say one thing you notice people doing on a walk.
levels.develop: Watch a place for ten minutes, and write three patterns.
levels.extend: Compare a pattern in two places, like home and somewhere new.

steps.title: Predict what will happen
steps.why: A prediction written down before the test is what makes it science, not a guess after the fact.
steps.kid: Your kid turns the pattern into a prediction, using the Make a prediction card: 'If I say hi first, about half of the people will answer.'
steps.you: Make your own prediction too, and write both down. Comparing them afterwards is half the fun.
ask: What do you think will happen?
Out of ten people, how many?
steps.tip: A number makes it testable. 'Most people' is hard to check. 'Six out of ten' isn't.

levels.explore: Guess yes or no: will people say hi back?
levels.develop: Predict how many out of ten will answer.
levels.extend: Predict, and write why you think so.

steps.title: Run a kind test
steps.why: The test only works if it's the same every time, and kind every time.
steps.kid: Your kid does one small, friendly thing to each person they cross, the same way every time, using the Kind tests card: say hi, smile, hold a door or wave.
steps.you: Stay right beside them. Keep it to public places and quick, friendly moments, nothing more.
ask: Are you doing it the same way each time?
What's the kindest way to run this test?
steps.tip: Same words, same smile, same distance. If you change the test halfway, the results won't mean much.

levels.explore: Say hi to five people on a walk, with a parent.
levels.develop: Test ten people the same way, on two different days.
levels.extend: Test one change, like smiling first versus not, and compare.

steps.title: Count what happens
steps.why: Feelings remember the one grumpy person. Tally marks remember everyone.
steps.kid: Your kid tallies each reaction in My people experiment page at the end of the guide, using the Reactions to count card: answered right away, looked surprised then answered, or no answer.
steps.you: Keep the counting honest, even when it's disappointing. Then count up the totals together.
ask: How many answered out of how many?
steps.tip: Count the in-between reactions too. A puzzled look before a hi is often the most interesting result.

levels.explore: Put a tally mark for each yes and each no.
levels.develop: Tally three kinds of reactions, and add them up.
levels.extend: Turn your tallies into fractions, and compare two days or two places.

steps.title: Explain the results
steps.why: The numbers say what happened. The explanation is where they learn something about people.
steps.kid: Your kid compares the results with their prediction and writes one possible reason, using the Explain it card. Then they plan what to test next.
steps.you: Offer kind explanations to consider: 'Maybe they're not unfriendly. Maybe they're just not used to it.'
steps.tip: Look for the kindest explanation that fits the numbers. It's usually closer to the truth than the first one.

levels.explore: Say if your guess was right or wrong, and why you think so.
levels.develop: Write your result, one reason for it, and your next test.
levels.extend: Write two possible reasons, and design a test that could tell them apart.

conclusion.headline: They see people as a question, not a verdict.
conclusion.text: Listen for the next time they notice something strange about how people act, and start with 'I wonder if...' instead of 'People are so...'. That's a scientist talking.
conclusion.celebrate: When they explain a result kindly, say: 'You didn't decide they were rude. You found out why. That's what scientists do.'
extensions: Run the same test at home and somewhere new, and compare
Test a second kind act, like holding a door, and count the results
Make a bar graph of all your experiments on one page
Ask a grandparent if people said hi more or less when they were young

signs: They say 'I wonder if...' about how people behave
They say hi first, even in a new place
They look for a kind explanation before deciding someone is rude
makeItReal: On your next walk somewhere new, decide together before you start: say hi first to everyone you cross, and count who answers. Compare it with your walks at home.

fromHome.text: Where we live, people always look at you and say hi when you cross them on the street or on a walking path, whether you're biking, walking or hiking. Once, in another province, we noticed people looked down instead. So we started saying hi to everyone, and noticed who would answer and who would ignore us. Some answered right away. Some looked at us first with a questioning face before answering, like they weren't used to saying hi.
